notes.meaning: Right after Israel rebelled and was sentenced to wander in the desert, God spoke to Moses again. He gave rules for what the people should do once they finally entered the Promised Land. This command gave the younger generation great hope, proving that God had not broken His promise to bring them into Canaan.

When the people arrived in the land, they were to bring animal sacrifices to God from their herds or flocks. These could be burnt offerings, gifts promised in a vow, freewill gifts, or offerings for regular feasts. The phrase 'pleasing aroma' shows that God gladly accepted sacrifices offered to Him with true devotion and thanksgiving.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the idea of a 'pleasing aroma' traces back to early ancient views where gods were believed to be literally fed or calmed by the smell of burning sacrifices.

notes.meaning: Whenever someone brought a young lamb or goat as a sacrifice, they were commanded to include grain and drink offerings. The worshiper added about two quarts of fine flour mixed with a quart of olive oil, plus a quart of wine poured out before God. Adding bread, oil, and wine turned the offering into a full sacred meal, expressing joyful gratitude for God's blessings.

When sacrificing a ram, the worshiper had to bring a larger amount of grain and wine. The offering required about four quarts of fine flour mixed with about a pint and a half of oil, along with an equal amount of wine. As the value of the main animal sacrifice increased, the accompanying gifts of praise grew with it.

A young bull was the largest standard sacrifice, so it required the largest grain and drink offerings. The worshiper presented about six quarts of fine flour mixed with two quarts of oil, along with two quarts of wine. The grain and oil were burned on the altar fire, creating a sweet smell that showed God's pleasure with their worship.

These exact amounts had to be given for every single bull, ram, lamb, or goat that was sacrificed. If a person or group presented several animals at once, the flour, oil, and wine had to be multiplied for each one. God wanted every offering to be handled with full care and generous thanksgiving.

Every native-born Israelite was required to follow this exact pattern whenever making an offering by fire. Worshipers were not free to invent their own rituals or leave out the grain and drink gifts. Worship had to be carried out faithfully, just as the Lord instructed.

If a foreigner lived among Israel and wanted to bring an offering to the Lord, they were welcome to do so. However, they were required to follow the very same instructions as native Israelites. This rule protected God's worship from idolatry while welcoming outsiders who sincerely turned to Him.

God established one single standard of worship for both native Israelites and foreign residents. Before the Lord, both stood on equal ground in how they approached Him with sacrifices. Many commentators note that this equality pointed ahead to the time when people from all nations would worship God together.

The Lord spoke to Moses again to give another law for life in Canaan. God stated that He was personally bringing them into the land, reinforcing His promise to complete what He started. This reassured the people that their wandering would come to an end.

Before eating the grain harvested in the new land, the people had to offer a gift to God. When they kneaded their first batch of dough, they were to take the first loaf and give it to the Lord's priests. By dedicating the very first bread from their homes, families turned everyday baking into an act of praise to God for providing their daily food.
